name: Tippecanoe Battlefield
source: folklore master
description: The 1811 battleground (F-001/016/152).

name: Ouiatanon site
source: folklore master
description: French post & Wea towns, S bank of the Wabash (F-054).

name: Prophetstown / Wabash-Tippecanoe confluence
source: folklore master
description: Mouth of the Tippecanoe (F-001).

name: Petrifying (tufa) Spring
source: PLSS notes
description: 'a remarkable Spring... elevated by a mass of petrified substance... 3.5 ft above the common level.'

name: Sulphur/Iron Water
source: PLSS notes
description: 'water sulphury or of Iron cast' past a Pine Creek crossing.

name: Pine Creek Falls & Mill Seat
source: PLSS notes
description: 'considerable falls... rock bottom, whetstone grit & slate stone'; a mill seat.

name: Mill Seat (30-in fall)
source: PLSS notes
description: 'a good mill seat, fall of 30 in nearly perpendicular.'

name: Muskrat Pond/Harbour
source: PLSS notes
description: Large pond/marsh complex; 'many Muskrat houses & Fish' (also T26N-R4W).

name: Racoon Pond
source: PLSS notes
description: Named pond on the W line of T26N-R5W.

name: Fish Pond
source: PLSS notes
description: Named pond by Muskrat Pond (T26N-R4W).

name: Rush Pond
source: PLSS notes
description: Named recurring wet pond, N-central T26N-R7W.

name: Grand Prairie (label)
source: PLSS notes
description: The great upper-Wabash prairie (also T25N-R4W, T26N-R7W).

name: Pretty Prairie (label)
source: PLSS notes
description: 'enter Pretty Prairie (so called)'.

name: Anderson's Grove
source: PLSS notes
description: Named timber grove (also T25N-R6W).

name: Walnut Grove
source: PLSS notes
description: 'This is called the Walnut grove'; a house nearby.

name: Finch's Grove
source: PLSS notes
description: 'known as Finches Grove, from the most influential man in the grove.'

name: White Oak Grove
source: PLSS notes
description: 'what is called the W. Oak grove.'

name: L'Isle a l'Aille (Wabash island)
source: PLSS notes
description: Named island in the Wabash (T25N-R2W plat).

name: Ridge dividing Wabash & Iroquois waters
source: PLSS notes
description: Low ridge (<25 ft) dividing the Wabash and Iroquois/Illinois drainages.

name: Burnet's Reserve (A. Burnett, Potawatomi)
source: PLSS plats/notes
description: On the Wabash by the battlefield; NW boundary = the plat's N50E line.

name: Burnett Reserve (1,280 ac)
source: PLSS plats/notes
description: SE of T25N-R3W, straddling into R2W.

name: Burnet 6-section Reserve (mouth of Flint Creek)
source: PLSS plats/notes
description: Six sections at the mouth of Flint Creek.

name: P. Langlois Reservation (1,250 ac)
source: PLSS plats/notes
description: 'Ten oldest children' of the French-Potawatomi trader Langlois, on the Wabash near Lafayette.

name: Wyandot Reserve 'Long Hair & others' (5 sec)
source: PLSS plats/notes
description: Wyandot reserve + village on the Wea Plain. Cross-ref F-153.

name: Jean B. Cicot Reserve (640 ac)
source: PLSS plats/notes
description: Cicot/Cicotte family reserve on the Wabash. Cross-ref F-121.

name: Z. Cicot's Children Reserve (960 ac)
source: PLSS plats/notes
description: On the Wabash (Carroll Co.). Cross-ref F-121.

name: Mary Chalilie/Challis Reserve (640 ac)
source: PLSS plats/notes
description: SW of T22N-R7W, straddling T21N-R7W (name uncertain).

name: Children of A. Bondie Reserve (2 sec)
source: PLSS plats/notes
description: Opposite L'Isle a l'Aille.

name: Mary Wells' Reserve (640 ac)
source: PLSS plats/notes
description: SW T25N-R2W near Stony Creek.

name: Connor's Reserve (J.W. & H. Connor, 1,920 ac)
source: PLSS plats/notes
description: Long tract on the SW bank of the Wabash.

name: Buffalo Trace (Vincennes Trace)
source: Wilson, Early Indiana Trails & Surveys (1919); Vincennes Trace
description: The great E-W artery of southern Indiana: Falls of the Ohio (New Albany) -> Paoli -> Shoals -> Vincennes. Worn first by migrating bison, then the main Native and pioneer road to the lower Wabash. (Loads its Part-A locked ID into the atlas.)

name: Red Banks Trail
description: Henderson KY ('Red Banks') -> Evansville -> Princeton -> Vincennes; near-due N-S, ~1 mi W of the R10/R11 line. Harmar's 1787 route.

name: Yellow Banks Trail
description: Rockport (Ohio R.) N through Spencer/Warrick/Pike to the Delaware summer camp at the forks of White R.; via Chrisney, Gentryville, Dale, Otwell; crossed the Patoka at a ford near Jasper. Delaware 'Weesoe Wusapinuk'.

name: Rome Trace
description: Rome (Perry Co., orig. 'Washington') NW via Fulda, Mariah Hill, N of Dale to the SW corner of Dubois Co.; lost at the Freeman line ~2 mi NE of Pleasantville; joined the Yellow Banks Trail near the Pike Co. line.

name: Shawnee Trace
source: Wilson 1919 pp.360,455
description: Southern Illinois -> Vincennes; two traces joined near the 'beauty spots' ~6 mi NW of Mt. Carmel IL. 'Shawnee' = 'Southerner'. Only incidentally in Indiana.

name: Salt Route (Salt Trace)
source: Wilson 1919 pp.396-397
description: Vincennes -> White R. crossing near Hazleton -> Patoka at John Severns' (3 mi N of Princeton) -> SW to the Wabash near the mouth of the Little Wabash -> the Illinois salt works (Saline Creek, nr Shawneetown). Crossed the Wabash 'just below New Harmony'.

name: Kibbey's Road
description: First road across the whole state: Cincinnati -> Vincennes (cut by Capt. E. Kibbey, 1799). Via Milan/Dearborn Co., Madison, New Lexington, Salem, French Lick, the forks of White R. ~201 mi. Became the north fork of the Buffalo trace.

name: Vallonia Trace
description: Vallonia (old fort, Jackson Co.) SE through Washington & Scott Cos. into Clark's Grant near the Pigeon Roost, to old Springville (nr Charlestown) and the Falls of the Ohio; crossed the Muscatatuck. The 'Aaron Burr cabin' stood on it.

name: Whetzel's Trace
source: Wilson 1919 pp.399-401
description: Jacob Whetzel's 1818 trace through the New Purchase: Laurel (Whitewater R., Franklin Co.) W ~60 mi to the West Fork of White R. at Waverly; ~7 mi below Rushville, 4 mi above Shelbyville, N of Boggstown. Permission from Delaware Chief Anderson.

name: Great Wabash Trail
source: Dunn/DeHart; PLSS
description: Principal Native N-S route following the Wabash (Vincennes-Ouiatanon-Kekionga). PLSS confirms the river corridor WAS the route; plotted along the Wabash.

name: Wabash-Maumee Portage (Kekionga)
source: Dunn Vol.I
description: The 'glorious gate' carrying-place between the Great Lakes (Maumee) and Wabash watersheds at Fort Wayne. Cross-ref F-049.

name: Great Sauk Trail
source: standard
description: Detroit-Chicago great trail across far N Indiana; clips N of the footprint.

name: Potawatomi Trail of Death (1838)
source: removal record
description: 1838 forced-removal route: Twin Lakes(Plymouth)->Logansport->Battle Ground vicinity->Williamsport->Danville IL->Kansas. Cross-ref F-040.

name: Wea Trail
source: Dunn/DeHart
description: Wea Plain <-> Ouiatanon/Wabash crossing.

name: Thorntown Trace
source: Wilson 1919; Dunn glossary (F-123)
description: Connector from the Wea towns/Ouiatanon SE to Thorntown (the Eel River Miami reserve, Boone Co.) and on toward central Indiana. Ties the Ouiatanon hub to the Thorntown band.

name: Strawtown / Lafayette Trace (Tecumseh's route)
source: Wilson 1919; IN.gov history blog (Lafayette/Strawtown Trace)
description: Prehistoric game trail -> Native trace: Delaware capital at Anderson -> ford at Strawtown (White R.) -> NW to the Wildcat & Wea prairies on the Wabash. The route Tecumseh rode from Anderson to Prophetstown; plowed under by the 1880s. FOOTPRINT-CONNECTING.

name: Mississinewa Trail
source: Wilson 1919; Dunn (cross-ref F-124/144)
description: Up the Mississinewa River from the Wabash at Peru through the Miami villages to the Mississinewa towns (site of the 1812 Mississinewa campaign); connects toward Lake Manitou.

name: Barnett's Road
source: PLSS plat T23N-R4W (labeled)
description: Named early road across the N of the Lafayette township toward Abraham Burnett's place/reserve.

name: Potawatomi-Miami Trail
source: potawatomi-miamitrail.org; standard
description: Fort Wayne-Chicago trade route (Maumee<->Lake Michigan via St. Joseph watershed/Elkhart Co.); distinct from the Sauk Trail.

name: Lafayette-Chicago Road
source: PLSS plat/notes T26N-R7W
description: State wagon road labeled 'Lafayette'<->'Chicago' on the T26N-R7W plat; crossed on many section lines through the Grand Prairie (Benton Co.).

name: Wabash-Rockville Wagon Road
source: PLSS notes
description: Wagon road 'supposed to lead from the Wabash to Rockville', NW course (T26N-R6W/R7W).

name: Strawtown-Kekionga Trail
source: IN.gov history blog; Wilson 1919
description: N-S trail crossing the Lafayette/Strawtown Trace at Strawtown and running to the Miami capital Kekionga (Fort Wayne).

name: Ouiatanon-Chicago Trace
source: Wilson 1919
description: Native trace NW from Ouiatanon across the Grand Prairie (Benton Co.) to the Kankakee and Chicago; the Indian precursor underlying the later Lafayette-Chicago wagon road (cross-ref TR-023).

name: St. Joseph-Kankakee Portage
source: Wilson 1919; Hulbert Vol.7; Baker 1899
description: St. Joseph R. landing near South Bend, SW ~4-5 miles across the prairie to the Kankakee marsh (near the sec. 7/8 line); the continental divide carry used by Marquette, La Salle, and the French voyageurs. 'German's Portage' was a variant landing a mile or more shorter. [Baker, The St. Joseph-Kankakee Portage, 1899]

name: Blue River Trace
source: Wilson 1919 pp.381-384
description: Ohio R. at Fredonia (mouth of Blue R.) N via Hardinsburg to the Buffalo trace near Samuel Hay's cabin on the W bank of Little Blue R. (~34.25 mi from Clark's Grant). Emigrant entry route after 1807.

name: Buck Creek Trace
source: Wilson 1919 p.357
description: Harrison Co. (R4E): Ohio R. -> Corydon -> the Buffalo trace; crossed the S fork of Buck creek twice. Squire Boone's mill and 'cave-sepulchre' nearby.

name: Illinois Trace
source: Wilson 1919 pp.361,420
description: The 'Old Buffalo trace' running W from Vincennes into Illinois (from Clark's Grant); the W line of the Vincennes tract crossed it. Clark's 1779 approach route is linked to it.

name: Michigan Road
source: Wilson 1919 pp.439-441
description: 1828-30 state road, 100 ft wide: Michigan City (Trail Creek/Lake Michigan) -> South Bend -> Rochester -> Logansport (Eel R.) -> Indianapolis -> Madison. Touches the footprint corridor at Logansport.

name: Vincennes-Fort Harrison Trail
source: Wilson 1919 p.361
description: Indian trail N from Vincennes, crossing the Freeman line near Carlisle, past Terre Haute to Fort Harrison (on the Wabash).

name: Fort Wayne-Nottawasepe Trail
source: Wilson 1919 p.432 (MI-IN line survey)
description: Indian trail from Fort Wayne NW to Nottawasepe (Michigan); crossed the state line ~6 mi W of the NE corner of LaGrange Co.

name: Coldwater-Fort Wayne Trail
source: Wilson 1919 p.432 (MI-IN line survey)
description: Indian trail between Coldwater (Michigan) and Fort Wayne; crossed the state line just N of Fremont, IN (near James Lake).

name: Chicago Portage
source: Hulbert, Historic Highways of America, Vol.7 'Portage Paths' (1903), Gutenberg #41179
description: The continental hinge Chicago R. (Lake Michigan) <-> Des Plaines/Illinois R. (Mississippi). Marquette wintered on it 1674-75; named in the 1795 Treaty of Greenville. The reason Chicago exists.

name: Fox-Wisconsin Portage ('The Grand Portage')
source: Hulbert, Historic Highways of America, Vol.7 'Portage Paths' (1903), Gutenberg #41179
description: Fox R. (Green Bay/Great Lakes) <-> Wisconsin R. (Mississippi) at present Portage, WI. Crossed by Nicollet (1634) and Joliet & Marquette (1673); guarded by Fort Winnebago.

name: Niagara Portage (Lake Erie <-> Lake Ontario)
source: Hulbert, Historic Highways of America, Vol.7 'Portage Paths' (1903), Gutenberg #41179
description: The carry around Niagara Falls between Lakes Ontario and Erie -- the great choke-point of the lower Lakes; long controlled by the Seneca and then contested by France and Britain.

name: Cuyahoga-Tuscarawas Portage ('the Portage Path')
source: Hulbert, Historic Highways of America, Vol.7 'Portage Paths' (1903), Gutenberg #41179
description: Lake Erie (Cuyahoga R.) <-> Ohio R. (Tuscarawas/Muskingum) at present Akron, OH; the 'Portage Path' was a surveyed treaty landmark (1785 Fort McIntosh line).

name: Scioto-Sandusky Portage
source: Hulbert, Historic Highways of America, Vol.7 'Portage Paths' (1903), Gutenberg #41179
description: Lake Erie (Sandusky R.) <-> Ohio R. (Scioto) -- the central Ohio carry linking the Lakes to the Ohio down the Scioto.

name: Miami-St. Mary's (Loramie) Portage
source: Hulbert, Historic Highways of America, Vol.7 'Portage Paths' (1903), Gutenberg #41179
description: Great Miami R. (Ohio R. system) <-> St. Mary's R. (Maumee/Lake Erie) at Loramie's store; the SW Ohio carry between the Ohio and the Lakes.

name: Chautauqua Portage
source: Hulbert, Historic Highways of America, Vol.7 'Portage Paths' (1903), Gutenberg #41179
description: Lake Erie <-> Chautauqua Lake -> Allegheny/Ohio (Mississippi system); the shortest Lakes-to-Ohio carry, used by the French 1753 to reach the Allegheny.

name: Presque Isle-French Creek Portage
source: Hulbert, Historic Highways of America, Vol.7 'Portage Paths' (1903), Gutenberg #41179
description: Lake Erie (Presque Isle) <-> Riviere aux Boeufs (French Creek) -> Allegheny; the French 1753 fort chain (Presque Isle -> Le Boeuf) carry.

name: Great Trail (tidewater -> Detroit)
source: Hinsdale, Archaeological Atlas of Michigan (1931), ch. 'Trails' | also in Hulbert Vol.2 Indian Thoroughfares (Ft Pitt->Big Beaver->Bolivar->Mohican John's Town->Sandusky->Detroit; Heckewelder 1796 map)
description: The principal E-W trunk: forks of the Ohio (Pittsburgh) -> Fort Laurens (Tuscarawas ford) -> Mohican John's Town -> Sandusky Bay -> Maumee Rapids (Perrysburg) -> Toledo -> Monroe -> Flat Rock -> Brownstown -> Detroit; N of Detroit it becomes the Saginaw & Mackinaw Trail. A Maumee branch entered Michigan at Morenci and joined the Chicago Trail at Allen.

name: Lake Erie Shore Trail
source: Hinsdale, Archaeological Atlas of Michigan (1931), ch. 'Trails' | also Hulbert Vol.2 (Niagara->Presque Isle->Sandusky->Detroit, 'second beach'; Heckewelder 1796)
description: South shore of Lake Erie: Toledo (where the Michigan trails converged) -> Sandusky Bay -> Cleveland -> Erie PA -> Buffalo/Niagara NY; closely followed by the modern lakeshore highway. Extends east as the Mohawk Trail to the Hudson.

name: Scioto Trail
source: Hinsdale, Archaeological Atlas of Michigan (1931), ch. 'Trails' | also Hulbert Vol.2 (Sandusky valley->Scioto->Ohio; Kanawha branch to Pt Pleasant; Filson/Hutchins maps)
description: Branched from the Great/Shore trails at Sandusky Bay, up the Sandusky R. to the portage, down the Scioto to the Ohio, then across Kentucky (Warriors' Path) to Cumberland Gap and the South. The copper-and-shell trade artery: Michigan copper south, marine shell north.

name: Montreal Trail (Detroit -> Prophetstown/Ouiatenon)
source: Hinsdale, Archaeological Atlas of Michigan (1931), ch. 'Trails' (Eddy 1816 & Hutchins 1778 maps)
description: THE Great Lakes land-link into the footprint: an old trail from Montreal following the Chicago Trail from Detroit, branching at Fort St. Joseph (Niles) and leading SOUTH to the Tippecanoe River, Prophet's Town, and Ouiatenon on the Wabash. From Ouiatenon, water route to New Orleans (Eddy: 1,871 mi). FOOTPRINT-CONNECTING.

name: Mahoning Trail
source: Hinsdale, Archaeological Atlas of Michigan (1931), ch. 'Trails' | also Hulbert Vol.2 (runners' bypass Ft Pitt->Beaver/Mahoning->Cuyahoga-Tuscarawas portage->Sandusky)
description: The most direct Detroit <-> forks-of-the-Ohio route: up the north bend of the Mahoning R. (E Ohio), then W to join the Great Trail near Sandusky Bay.

name: Saginaw & Mackinaw Trail
source: Hinsdale, Archaeological Atlas of Michigan (1931), ch. 'Trails'
description: Detroit -> Pontiac -> Flint -> Saginaw R. -> up the Tittabawassee to Edenville, where it forked for the Grand Traverse region and for Cheboygan/the Straits of Mackinac. Followed by the Dixie Highway from Toledo through Detroit, Pontiac, Flint.

name: Grand River Trail
source: Hinsdale, Archaeological Atlas of Michigan (1931), ch. 'Trails'
description: Detroit -> Grand Rapids (mouth of the Grand), through Oakland, Livingston, Ingham, Ionia, Kent counties; followed the Cedar R. much of the way. Leaves Detroit as Grand River Avenue / the Grand River Road; a trail network fanned out at the Grand Rapids.

name: Territorial Trail
source: Hinsdale, Archaeological Atlas of Michigan (1931), ch. 'Trails'
description: Crossed the Chicago/Sauk Trail at Ypsilanti, through Ann Arbor, the centers of Jackson & Calhoun counties, branching to Kalamazoo (uniting with the Chicago Trail in SE Berrien Co.) and to the mouths of the St. Joseph (St. Joseph) and Kalamazoo (Saugatuck).

name: Potawatomi Trail (Huron River, Michigan)
source: Hinsdale, Archaeological Atlas of Michigan (1931), ch. 'Trails'
description: Followed the Huron R. from its mouth (Lake Erie) up to Portage Lake (Washtenaw/Livingston line), crossing the Chicago/Sauk Trail at Ypsilanti and passing Ann Arbor. Distinct from the Fort Wayne-Chicago Potawatomi-Miami Trail (TR-022).

name: Mackinaw-St. Joseph Shore Trail
source: Hinsdale, Archaeological Atlas of Michigan (1931), ch. 'Trails'
description: Down the east shore of Lake Michigan: Mackinaw -> the Traverse bays -> Manistee/Mason/Oceana shore -> South Haven -> mouth of the St. Joseph (St. Joseph); below St. Joseph it touched the shore villages and JOINED THE SAUK TRAIL IN INDIANA, connecting for Chicago. FOOTPRINT-CONNECTING.

name: Harmar's Road (1790)
source: Hulbert, Historic Highways Vol.8 'Military Roads of the Mississippi Basin: The Conquest of the Old Northwest' (1904), Gutenberg #41167
description: Harmar's 1790 campaign march, Fort Washington (Cincinnati) NW to the Maumee towns at Kekionga (Fort Wayne): via Lebanon, Fish-pot Ford (Little Miami), old Chillicothe, Mad R. near New Carlisle, Troy, Piqua (Great Miami), Loramie's Creek, St. Marys. Followed Clark's 1782 trace out of Cincinnati; Hardin's ambush fell on the Kickapoo path near the Eel R. ~11 mi from Fort Wayne.

name: Wayne's Trace & the fort chain (1791-94)
source: Hulbert, Historic Highways Vol.8 'Military Roads of the Mississippi Basin: The Conquest of the Old Northwest' (1904), Gutenberg #41167 + standard campaign histories
description: The military road and fort chain of the Old Northwest conquest: Fort Washington -> Ft. Hamilton -> Ft. St. Clair (Eaton) -> Ft. Jefferson -> Ft. Greene Ville -> Ft. Recovery (St. Clair's 1791 defeat) -> Ft. Adams -> Ft. Defiance (Auglaize-Maumee) -> down the Maumee to Fallen Timbers & Ft. Meigs (the Rapids). Wayne built Fort Wayne at Kekionga, 1794.

name: Hull's Road (1812)
source: Hulbert, Historic Highways Vol.8 'Military Roads of the Mississippi Basin: The Conquest of the Old Northwest' (1904), Gutenberg #41167 + War-of-1812 histories
description: Hull's 1812 march to Detroit, the chief supply road of the NW theatre: Dayton/Urbana -> Ft. McArthur (Kenton) -> Ft. Findlay -> Ft. Meigs (Maumee Rapids) -> Brownstown -> Detroit.

name: Cuyahoga-Muskingum Trail (Old Muskingum Trail)
source: Hulbert, Historic Highways Vol.2 'Indian Thoroughfares' (1902)
description: Lake Erie <-> Ohio R. through the Delaware country: mouth of the Cuyahoga (Cleveland) -> the great portage to the Tuscarawas (Akron) -> down the Tuscarawas past the Crossing-place of the Muskingum (Bolivar) to the Delaware capital Gosh-goshing (Coshocton) -> down the Muskingum to Marietta.

name: Miami Trail
source: Hulbert, Historic Highways Vol.2 'Indian Thoroughfares' (1902)
description: War-and-trade path: the Great/Little Miami valleys converging to cross the Ohio near the mouth of the Miami (North Bend/Cincinnati), then through the Licking and Kentucky valleys to the Cumberland watershed; a branch joins the Warriors' Path through Cumberland Gap into Cherokee country.

name: Maumee / 'Miami-of-the-Lake' Trail
source: Hulbert, Historic Highways Vol.2 'Indian Thoroughfares' (1902) (Hutchins map 1764)
description: Scioto -> Maumee connector: from Lower Shawnees Town (mouth of the Scioto) NW on the watershed between the Scioto and the two Miamis to the Maumee valley and the Miami town at Kekionga (Fort Wayne) -- the road on toward the Lake Michigan and Superior country.

name: Venango Path
source: Hulbert, Historic Highways Vol.2 'Indian Thoroughfares' (1902)
description: The main landward Fort Pitt -> Lake Erie route and French-fort line: Fort Pitt N on the Allegheny/Beaver watershed to Fort Venango (Franklin), up French Creek (Riviere aux Boeufs) to Fort Le Boeuf (Waterford) and the portage to Fort Presque Isle (Erie).

name: Scioto-Beaver Trail
source: Hulbert, Historic Highways Vol.2 'Indian Thoroughfares' (1902)
description: Second in Western importance to the Great Trail: Lower Shawnees Town up the Scioto/Tuscarawas to the Delaware country near Coshocton, then the Tuscarawas-Ohio watershed to 'Painted Post' and the Pennsylvania frontier at the Beaver. Traversed by Christopher Gist for the Ohio Company.

name: Scioto-Monongahela Trail
source: Hulbert, Historic Highways Vol.2 'Indian Thoroughfares' (1902)
description: Scioto country <-> the 'Long House' via the lower Ohio: Lower Shawnees Town E across Fairfield/Perry Cos. to Wallace Ridge and 'Big Rock', S to the Ohio opposite the mouth of the Little Kanawha (Belpre), crossing at Parkersburg, by Dry Ridge to the Monongahela. Tecumseh's party marched part of it.

name: Iroquois Trail (Great Central Trail)
source: Hulbert, Historic Highways Vol.2 'Indian Thoroughfares' (1902) (Guy Johnson map 1771)
description: The spine of the Six Nations' Long House and one of the longest independent thoroughfares on the continent: Hudson R. below Albany -> up the Mohawk valley -> Ft Stanwix (Rome) -> Oneida -> Onondaga (Syracuse, the council fire) -> Cayuga (Auburn) -> N of the Finger Lakes -> Seneca country (Canandaigua, Batavia) -> Niagara R. just S of the falls. Became the Genesee Rd / NY Central corridor. [NORTHEAST / Laurie's NY]

name: Old Connecticut Path
source: Hulbert, Historic Highways Vol.2 'Indian Thoroughfares' (1902)
description: Boston/Cambridge -> Marlborough -> Grafton -> Oxford -> Springfield -> Albany; the Bay colonists' road to the Hudson, ~ the Boston & Albany RR alignment. [NORTHEAST]

name: New Connecticut Path
source: Hulbert, Historic Highways Vol.2 'Indian Thoroughfares' (1902)
description: Parallel to the Old Connecticut Path: Cambridge -> Worcester -> Albany. [NORTHEAST]

name: Kittanning Path
source: Hulbert, Historic Highways Vol.2 'Indian Thoroughfares' (1902)
description: A preeminent traders' route over the Alleghenies: Kittanning on the Allegheny -> Kittanning Gorge/Point (nr Hollidaysburg) -> up the Juniata (Water Street, Alexandria) -> across the ridges -> Susquehanna/Carlisle -> Philadelphia. Became Forbes's Road (1758). [NORTHEAST/Appalachian]

name: Nemacolin's Path
source: Hulbert, Historic Highways Vol.2 'Indian Thoroughfares' (1902)
description: The 'bloody thoroughfare' VA/MD traffic converged on: Wills Creek (Ft Cumberland) -> Little Crossings -> Great Meadows -> Gist's Plantation (Mt Braddock) -> Stewart's Crossing (Connellsville) -> the forks of the Ohio (Pittsburgh). Became Washington's Rd, Braddock's Rd, the Cumberland/National Rd. [NORTHEAST/Appalachian]

name: Virginia Warriors' Path
source: Hulbert, Historic Highways Vol.2 'Indian Thoroughfares' (1902)
description: The great N-S war trail in the trough between the Blue Ridge and Cumberland ranges: Shenandoah/New R. valley -> Cumberland Gap -> Crab Orchard -> Danville -> the Falls of the Ohio (Louisville), on toward the Mississippi. Became Boone's Wilderness Road. [NORTHEAST/Appalachian->South]

name: Indian trail (confluence)
source: PLSS notes T24N-R3W
description: 'an Indian trail' logged in the Tippecanoe meander at the Wabash-Tippecanoe mouth.

name: Old Indian trail (deep hollow)
source: PLSS notes T26N-R7W
description: 'old Indian trail N&S, a deep hollow' logged on the line btw Secs 25&36.

name: Kickapoo Village (Wabash)
source: PLSS plats/notes
description: 'an Indian village occupied by Kickapoos' on the Wabash bottom.

name: Wyandot Village (Long Hair)
source: PLSS plats/notes
description: Drawn village on the Wyandot reserve. Cross-ref F-153.

name: French/Potawatomi 'Village des...'
source: PLSS plats/notes
description: Village by the Langlois reserve on the Wabash.

name: Morris Trading House ('Morris' landing')
source: PLSS plats/notes
description: 'a Trading house formerly used by a Mr. Morris'; drawn as a building on the plat.

name: Wabash River
source: PLSS plats/notes (meander tables)
description: The main stem; surveyed meander banks across the county. Approx course from PLSS crossings (NE Carroll Co. -> SW past Lafayette toward Attica).

name: Tippecanoe River
source: PLSS plats/notes
description: Chief northern tributary; meanders S/SW to join the Wabash at the mouth in T24N-R3W Sec 8 (the confluence by Prophetstown). Islands incl. a cluster in T26N-R3W Sec 3.

name: Pine Creek (Big Pine Creek)
source: PLSS notes (named 'Pine Creek'/'Big Pine Creek'/'Pine River')
description: Major western drainage, SE course; whetstone-grit falls & mill seats in T21N-R7W. Flows toward the Wabash near Attica.

name: Wild Cat Creek
source: PLSS notes
description: Crosses the Wea Plain NW/W toward the Wabash. Named in PLSS notes; the Prophet's refuge after the 1811 battle.

name: Wea Creek (Weeawe)
source: PLSS notes
description: Miami-named creek entering the Wabash from the SE; the only cultural name in the Ouiatanon township notes.

name: Pouceaupichieux Creek
source: PLSS notes
description: French-derived creek name; enters the Wabash from the SW (spelling approximate).

name: Flint Creek
source: PLSS notes
description: Creek at whose mouth the 6-section Burnet reserve sat (T22N-R6W).

name: Stony Creek
source: PLSS notes
description: Named on the T25N-R2W plat near Mary Wells' Reserve.

name: Little Pine Creek
source: PLSS notes
description: Named creek, SE course (T24N-R6W).

name: Brosher Creek
source: PLSS notes
description: Named creek in T21N-R7W (spelling uncertain).

name: Burnett's Creek
source: DeHart/battle accounts; PLSS
description: Willow-lined stream on the W/NW edge of the Tippecanoe battlefield; Harrison's army camped on the oak rise above it the night of Nov 6-7, 1811 (rear line guarded the creek). Flows SW past Battle Ground to the Wabash. Named for the Burnett family -- almost certainly the metis Potawatomi Burnetts (cf. Burnet's Reserve RS-01, same township); eponym not stated in battle histories (VERIFY). Cross-ref F-001/016/152/155.
